what: The ideas register: the core ideas the second edition is made of, one node each, with where each came from (provenance), which 2018 chapters it answers, which proposed chapter it goes to, and its state. Authored by the librarian on 18 October 2026 from the nine co-written articles, the seven decisions, the newsroom survey and the 49 articles it brings, and the six briefs; extended whenever a new article is processed. A state is 'candidate' until Dinis accepts it (read, comment, decide); 'accepted' here means Dinis said it in a co-written article as his own position, and the decision on the text is still to be recorded in the vault by the editor.

kinds.frame: a way of seeing the whole book uses
kinds.claim: something the book asserts and must back
kinds.method: a way of working the reader can copy
kinds.evidence: a number or a source the book cites
kinds.process: how the book itself is made; the last part, or not the book at all

destinations.this-edition: in the second edition's first release
destinations.next-version: after the first release of the second edition
destinations.the-process: about how the book is made: the site, the workflow, not the reader's text

states.accepted: Dinis said it, in an article or a memo; to record in the vault as a decision on the text
states.drafting: the editor is writing it in the vault
states.declined: not doing it, with the reason
states.deferred: later, to a named version or book

ideas.title: A graph is a network of nodes and edges, not a diagram
ideas.statement: Some readers think a graph is a picture with boxes; the book means a network, nodes and the edges between them, and shows it with visualisations. Of the three things people mean by the word (networks for analysis, graph databases for storage, semantics for meaning) the book uses the first and the third.

ideas.title: Graphs nest, and so does the world: groups of groups are the abstraction layers we think in
ideas.statement: Fractal graphs, graphs of graphs: there is no top and no bottom, only the altitude you look from and how much definition you load there. Even nature can be seen as a gigantic graph, from systems to molecules to photons; groups of groups form the natural abstraction layers, which is how we think.

ideas.statement: A graph has no front page and no top, so you never need to feel overwhelmed: it does not matter where you start or whether you go straight in the right direction; it matters that you start, connect the dots and get movement. A path only makes sense afterwards.

ideas.statement: The 2018 outline Graphs has four bullets that are the new chapter in miniature, and two published chapters, Dot Language (drawing the diagrams software never has) and AST (a syntax tree as 'a graph representation of source code'), are examples to place inside it.

ideas.title: Source code is a fractal semantic graph, and a review should read every layer of it
ideas.statement: Stories, flows, components, classes, methods and calls, the syntax tree: each layer is a graph with its own vocabulary. Naming a node and its verb is now cheap, so a change can be diffed at every altitude: a refactor moves the bottom and leaves the top still; a fix is a story holding again; the blast radius is the climb from the methods touched to the stories that can reach them. The only honest answer to AI-generated code that breaks something three packages away.

What to bring: next to the 2018 AST chapter

ideas.notes: The worked example is the sgit tool read as layered graphs, published as a vault with the read key on the page; the stories are hand-written and the example runs nothing. The numbers on the review burden (GitClear, DORA, Stack Overflow, Veracode) are in the article.

ideas.title: A graph is trustworthy not because it is right but because it is where users, experts and tests can correct it
ideas.statement: A model's first reading of anything will be partly wrong; the plan does not need it right. It needs layers someone knows and predictions something can check: users confirm the top, experts their own layer, tests the execution, and every correction is a commit with a name on it. Patterns in the shape are findings in themselves.

sources.where: What makes it work is reality

ideas.title: There is a company in this: a code review that reads every layer, for somebody to build
ideas.statement: Say the business plainly: a review attached to a repository that keeps the layered graph current per commit and shows each change at every altitude, sold to anyone generating code faster than they can review it, and to teams whose threat model and component layer should be the same graph. What is defensible is the record and the loop, not the model; the scripts are Apache-2.0 and a founder needs a second language and a first customer, not permission.
ideas.notes: One of the business plans published for founders on sgit.ai; an example of the book's advice to start a company from a published plan.

ideas.title: The voice is not a setting: a corpus, a memo, a short list of rules, and a reader who corrects
ideas.statement: An agent sounds like its author because of four inputs: a corpus of the author's writing that defines the vocabulary; voice memos that carry how the author thinks, in the order they thought it; a short list of wording rules, each learned from one correction; and the author reading everything before and after it goes live. Take any one away and it stops working. The method transfers; the voice does not.

ideas.title: Speak it, do not type it: a memo carries how you got there, a brief only what to write
ideas.statement: A typed brief is already edited into someone else's register; a voice memo keeps the rhythm, the tangents and the order the ideas came in, and the agent keeps those phrases rather than paraphrasing them. The tangent is not noise; it is the connection the author made. An article from a memo sounds like its author; one from a typed brief sounds like a careful assistant.

ideas.title: A wording correction is made once and enforced; a content correction is new thinking every time
ideas.statement: 'No em-dashes' is a rule an agent can keep; 'sound more human' is not. Each jarring word becomes a line in the behaviour policy, restored after every summary and checked by the validator, so the corrections move from language to content, which is the measure that the voice is working.

ideas.title: Memory is not a spectator sport: it is context management, many memories, fractal, published and shared
ideas.statement: The industry's picture is one store everything is pumped into and retrieved from by similarity. Dinis's is the opposite: memory is deciding what an agent needs in its window now, and no more, because context costs tokens and attention; it is many memories, each with its own vocabulary; it is fractal, principles in a few kilobytes at the top and code at the bottom; it is published and open so an agent can fetch, quote and cite; and it is shared through vaults so a session can end and the next picks up from the same files. The field arrived at files too: a plain filesystem beat a graph memory on the benchmark.

ideas.title: Publish, and your published work becomes your agents' memory, with a URL for every claim
ideas.statement: Open source and Creative Commons are not a licensing preference: they are what makes a memory usable by an agent. The more you publish, the more the next session stands on and the less it has to be told; a public page can be fetched, a public quote cited, a public graph loaded, a public vault cloned with a key that is itself public. For the reader: write in public, and your future self and your agents inherit it.

ideas.title: Stale pages become false memories, so a memory must say where each thing came from and name its own errors
ideas.statement: A shared memory made by agents and people becomes a rumour mill unless every item carries its source; and it goes stale: the session that wrote the article found four stale claims about its own estate and fixed two, measuring the rest at build time rather than remembering them. A memory that hides its errors is the thing to argue against. 'If the reality document doesn't list it, it does not exist.'

ideas.title: The file system is the database: load, extract, transform, save, and keep every intermediate as a file
ideas.statement: A database server is a large, stateful, always-on thing to provision, secure, back up and pay for, and most of what it holds would be happy as files. LETS loads state, works on it and saves every stage back as files you can version, diff and read: a cache, a database and an audit trail in one, with git as its history. Two real database engines now run in the reader's browser over the site's own JSON.

sources.where: Step one: the file system is the database

ideas.title: No server, by design: retire the back end too, and keep only commodity servers
ideas.statement: After the database, the back end: the newsroom's personas, reading meter, payments, versions and databases all run in the browser, and what is left on the server side is a product someone else runs (static hosting, a vault server that stores only ciphertext, a payment link, DNS, a build pipeline). A constraint did the design: the vault server cannot read anything, so the logic had to go where the key is. It scales without its complexity scaling, ships fast (114 releases in eleven days), and lines up with sovereignty, privacy, explainability and determinism. The one real limit: a secret the reader must not hold cannot live in their browser.

sources.where: Step two: the back end goes too; Not 'no servers': commodity servers
It scales without the complexity scaling; It ships fast; Sovereignty, privacy, explainability, determinism

ideas.notes: Answers the 2018 outline Serverless ('the path to Serverless', 'important to understand the limitations') from the other side: not Lambda, no back end at all. Not a claim that servers are bad: a trading system or a bank's ledger needs shared, live, authoritative state.

ideas.title: Security experience is what lets you ship with known gaps: list them, match them to the reader, say what would change the call
ideas.statement: A design with no server has gaps, and the honest thing is to write them down: a reader can edit a balance, start again in a private window, credit themselves; every one changes a number only the cheater sees. Closing them would bring back accounts, a database, a server and a sign-up wall. Security judgement is asking who you are protecting against, accepting what does not match the threat, and naming the condition that would make the gaps unacceptable.
ideas.notes: The synthetic readers found no security problem but found the cost of the gaps in the words on the page ('below zero' read as a debt).

ideas.title: Open source is why it is easy to throw your own technology away
ideas.statement: When everything you build is open, there is no moat you have to keep using and no part of the stack to protect from replacement; you can be the first to replace what you wrote when something better appears. The habit is to ask of every component whether it still earns its place, and open source removes the one bad reason to say yes: that you built it.

ideas.title: Tools changed everything: the model answers with a request, the program runs it, and the result goes into the next request
ideas.statement: The first ChatGPT and Claude had only their training, a compression of the world that stopped at a date. Now a model can return a tool call instead of an answer (search the web, call a service, read a file); the harness decides whether to run it, runs it, adds the result to the conversation and sends it all back. The model never runs a tool, which is where the control lives. From no tools in November 2022 to an open standard for them in November 2024.

ideas.title: The model remembers nothing between requests: every request carries the whole conversation, which is why there is a context window
ideas.statement: There is no memory, only a cache that saves work; the model starts from the prompt it receives, so it has to receive all of it, and a long chat costs more every turn. When an assistant 'remembers' you, it is saved notes put back into the prompt.

ideas.title: Long chats are compressed into a lower-resolution summary, so details drop out: work in many focused threads with named agents
ideas.statement: When a conversation gets too long it is replaced by a summary, and what the summary leaves out is gone unless it is in a file; the newsroom's session was summarised eighteen times in a month, keeping 1.7% each time. So keep the rules in a file printed back after every summary, and work in lots of separate mini agents, each with a name and one job, which is how the agentic inbox runs.
